newsitem.title: CANADA: Winnipeg puts 10,000 on Red River flood alert.
newsitem.headline: Winnipeg puts 10,000 on Red River flood alert.

text.p: About 10,000 Winnipeg residents went on evacuation alert on Wednesday as emergency workers pumped water from leaking dikes and fortified others protecting Manitoba's capital from the surging Red River.
"We're not going to sit here and tell you we're not worried," Winnipeg Mayor Susan Thompson said. "We're worried about the people on the rivers and low lying areas."

About 8,800 residents have already fled their homes as the bloating Red River seeped through dikes shielding five city streets on Wednesday, while workers feverishly pumped water out. The river was expected to crest at the city of 650,000 people as early as Thursday night.
The western Canadian province's biggest city is protected by a 29-mile (47-km) ditch parting the rising "Red Sea" and a 25-mile (40-km) dike southwest of the city that was completed on Wednesday.
"The dike is complete and the most vulnerable part has no water against it," Manitoba flood liaison engineer Larry Whitney said.
Engineers said Red River head waters might reach Winnipeg within six hours of any breach of that dike, raising the river's crest two feet (61 cm) above its forecast peak downtown within 40 hours.

"I think government leaders are right to take precautionary measures. Nobody wants to take any chances with an unprecedented flood here, but this worst case scenario is a very remote possibility," Whitney said.

The Red River, the largest of Winnipeg's four rivers, swelled to 22 times its normal flow this month as record winter snows melted. The flood is Manitoba's worst since 1852 and has inundated 800 square miles (2,072 sq km).
The white-capped waves of the Red River have displaced almost 29,000 Canadians and 50,000 Americans so far.
Anne Barton left her south Winnipeg home on Tuesday, only to be evacuated from her in-laws' home on Wednesday morning as flood water seeped through a 16-foot (5-metre) earthen dike.
"I'm trying to get my kids out and the stuff that we had packed up," Barton said as she left the neighbourhood.
Residents of 62 homes on her street may be allowed back when soldiers and workers finish sandbagging a seeping culvert.
"I don't believe anyone can overreact in this situation. If it saves a life, it's worth it," Manitoba Emergency Management executive coordinator Harold Clayton said.
Two boys and a man were presumed drowned last week in rising waters and another man died of a heart attack while sandbagging his south Winnipeg home on Saturday.
Soldiers rescued 37 people from Ste. Agathe, a town of 477 residents 20 miles (32 km) south of Winnipeg, as a six-foot (two-metre) wall of water submerged the town early on Tuesday.
Another foot of water filled Ste. Agathe as the river crested there on Wednesday.

"I'll probably get out there by helicopter tomorrow," Ste. Agathe Reeve (mayor) Bob Stefaniuk said. "You can see there's a deep concern among the evacuees. They're disappointed, they say things like: 'Gee, we tried and we didn't win.'"
Winnipeg's mayor on Wednesday ordered crews to add two more feet (61 cm) of sandbags to parts of the city's 75-mile (120-km) permanent earthen dike.
It should take two to three days to add one million sandbags to the ring dike, Winnipeg chief flood engineer Doug McNeil said.
